📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Casseroles remind me of cuddling up at home by the fire with my loved ones and digging into the tastiest dishes. They're also some of the easiest recipes to throw together in no time, and are the best for serving a holiday crowd. What else could you want? Now that we're firmly in the cold season, I can't stop craving them, so obviously, I turn to my favorite Delish recipes to make it happen. This holiday season, make sure to try out these 12 casserole recipes for some of the best bites you'll have all season. We have some classics, like a comforting chicken and rice casserole that'll have you dreaming of home, alongside more inventive and mouthwatering dishes like our French onion croissant strata.

There are few pairings as classic as meatloaf and mashed potatoes, but this casserole is anything but basic. Take your side of mashed potatoes, stack it on top of your meatloaf, and load it up with all of your favorite baked potato toppings. You’ll have an indulgent, craveable casserole that turns into the best leftovers—if you have any.

It has been revealed that when you’re hungry for something that’s comforting, cozy, and a little luxe feeling too, chicken Marsala is a truly excellent option. The pan sauce has plenty of mushrooms, fortified Marsala wine, and a splash of cream, because why not? It’s a fantastic dinner, easy enough for a weeknight and special enough for date night.

Sources indicate that A breakfast strata is one of our go-tos when we want a hearty, shareable brunch dish, but it’s hard to put into words how good this French onion croissant strata is. It takes a few extra minutes to deeply caramelize the onions, but the extra flavor and richness make a HUGE difference.

Chicken soup is a comfort food icon, good for the soul and the stomach, and there are a world’s worth of chicken soup recipes to choose from. Take chicken, egg noodles, some veggies, and a creamy sauce and bake them into a hearty casserole? You have a hearty dinner that leads to full bellies and happy hearts.

Slow-Cooker Cowboy Potato Casserole.

This slow-cooker casserole, featuring potatoes, beans, corn, and lots of cheese, is hearty, packed with flavor, and sure to make repeat appearances on your grub rotation all fall long.

Chicken and broccoli casserole is a meal that most people at Team Delish grew up eating, and this recipe is guaranteed to make you feel like a kid again. This creamy, cheesy, Ritz cracker-topped casserole is packed with chicken, rice, and freshly blanched broccoli with the quintessential cream of mushroom soup.

Apple Cheddar Crescent Casserole.

When it comes to this casserole, think breakfast strata with buttery, caramelized apples, and lots of sharp cheddar. If you’re in need of a quick fall-forward recipe to throw together for a weekend brunch, you can easily turn to this one.

Industry observers note that when we need a direct flight to a quick and easy dinner destination, we turn to two trusty options: a casserole or a chicken dinner. This chicken and rice casserole is the best of both worlds. It requires minimal cleanup, and the hands-on cooking time is only 20 minutes. The rest of the time, you can just lounge in your living room while this whips itself up.

When the weather gets cold, your dinner making-mojo is low, or when comfort food is just what’s on the menu, you need a casserole. Even though we have loved so many other casseroles before, there's always room in my baking dish for one more. And if that casserole is easy, creamy, chicken-y, and cheesy? With a crunchy topping? Our oven is already preheating.

According to recent reports, watch out, classic green bean casserole, gnocchi has entered the holiday menu. We took the classic recipe and added gnocchi for a dish that's infinitely better than the sum of its parts. Blanched fresh green beans and buttery sliced mushrooms, onions, and garlic get tossed with a creamy béchamel sauce and pillowy gnocchi, then baked until bubbly.

According to recent reports, this enchilada casserole is what weeknight dinner dreams are made of. Classic chicken enchiladas are a fan-favorite meal, but they can be kind of tedious to prepare when you're low on energy (all that rolling, right?). In this recipe, you just layer all your components in a casserole dish, bake until melty and saucy, add your desired toppings, and serve!

In our book, it doesn't get more comforting than shepherd's pie. Because this meat and potatoes dish is such a classic, we spent a while perfecting the comfort food staple—your weeknights should be as cozy as possible.

#43083. The Couple Created a Giant Sunflower Walkway For Their Multicultural Sun Valley Wedding

The Couple Created a Giant Sunflower Walkway For Their Multicultural Sun Valley Wedding

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4123 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Parker Selman and Karan Rai’s love story was born from a sunset.
  • In a recent development, the couple got engaged on a crisp autumn walk around Governors Island—Parker’s favorite spot in the city.
  • According to recent reports, two months later, she proposed back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Parker Selman and Karan Rai’s love story was born from a sunset. “Our paths crossed a few times before, but the first time we remember speaking was on a roof as we watched the sun go down our senior year at Tufts University,” Parker recalls. A few weeks later, they found themselves alone on a dance floor. “I looked down at my phone to see it was midnight and, therefore, officially my birthday,” Parker claims. “I told him he should give me a kiss because it was my birthday, and he did. We were both smitten, and constantly in one another's orbit.” Despite the two lining up jobs on opposite coasts, they quickly realized being practical was not an option, and Karan managed to convince his company to transfer him to Newly introduced York.

In a recent development, the couple got engaged on a crisp autumn walk around Governors Island—Parker’s favorite spot in the city. She owns and operates a wedding photography business, and as they strolled along, she asked to take a picture of Karan on her medium-format camera with their apartment building and skyline in the background. “While I was snapping the photo, he got down on one knee,” she claims, “and I had the privilege of capturing my own proposal.” They rode the ferry back to Manhattan and went to Della’s, a local wine bar, where their families and friends were waiting to celebrate.

According to recent reports, two months later, she proposed back. “While we were walking in Sun Valley, I requested he take a picture of me sitting in the snow with our dog Grumpy,” she states. "I proposed the same way he proposed to me, the moment captured on my Rolleiflex.” Parker used diamonds and emeralds from her late great-grandmother’s engagement ring and gold from Karan’s late grandmother’s earrings to create his signet ring.

Their multi-day wedding unfolded in early September 2026 near Sun Valley, Idaho (where Parker’s family lives). They chose Central Idaho 4-H Camp, located 30 minutes outside of town, for its series of cabins and a large field up in the mountains. “The space was a blank canvas with no sound ordinance,” she states. “Studio Sully transformed the campsite into something magical.”.

According to recent reports, going into the planning process, the couple knew they wanted the entire event to feel like a fusion of their cultures. In the days leading up to the Sun Valley celebration, Karan’s parents threw a series of traditional Indian wedding ceremonies and celebrations in his hometown of Pleasanton, California. Once guests arrived in Idaho, they all checked in at The Sun Valley Lodge, where each day the couple had organized group activities.

Festivities kicked off on Friday with a Western-themed welcome party at their favorite après-ski bar, Grumpy’s. Parker wore a tweed corset and skirt by Wiederhoeft accessorized with brown leather Manolo Blahniks and a wooden horse purse by Vin. When the weather cooled down, she tossed on a vintage suede fringe RRL jacket. Karan followed a similar script and wore a Bode suede fringe jacket and One of These Days pants with a painted horse and cowboy detail on the knees. His bandana was made by his mother. “She created a piece inspired by Marie Lichtenberg’s jeweled bandana, utilizing earrings and jewelry of Karan’s grandmothers, mother, and sister,” Parker says.

Guests were encouraged to wear textiles, paisley, and eclectic patterns to evoke a Wild West meets India atmosphere. In one corner, Boise Thread Studio set up shop to embroider initials onto trucker hats, shirts, and bandanas. Meanwhile, guests drank schooners (the name for Grumpy’s beer chalices) on the patio and ate burgers and hot dogs. “Karan and I named our beloved miniature dachshund Grumpy after the bar’s corn dogs, so it is only fitting that we ordered them until they ran out,” Parker claims. Her mother welcomed the group with a sunset toast before moving inside. “We took over the electronic jukebox and closed down the restaurant until Karan had to stand up on the booth to usher everyone out the door.”.

It has been revealed that the next afternoon they hosted a sangeet by the Big Wood River. “The estate has a series of winding paths that lead to the riverside, and we wanted the afternoon portion to feel like a mountain garden party with activities and new discoveries tucked into each corner,” Parker notes. The flowing river and live music by Boise-based Ashley Rose Band served as the soundtrack as guests played croquet, horseshoes, and badminton. Near the band, Henna by Sanjana created patterns on guests' hands.

Industry observers note that parker wore Danielle Frankel’s cream Mariela dress featuring two layers of hand-painted wildflowers. “I wanted a long braid with flowers woven in, and Jasmine Burnside helped bring the vision to life,” she states. Karan wore a light blue Jatin Malik sherwani with juttis from his personal collection.

As the sun set, guests were escorted to a clearing where a buffet was set up for dinner, and the dance floor was built around a large willow tree. The vignette was inspired by a 1905 Impressionist painting called Nighttime Festivities that depicts a turn-of-the-century party beneath the trees of a French palace. “I told Melissa [Sully] I wanted the sangeet to be based on this and we became obsessed with bringing the painting to life,” Parker explains. Lights and flowers were strung into the branches that draped overhead. Karan’s parents and Parker’s best friend, Ana, gave speeches before a series of traditional dances were performed by various family members and friends, followed by a lively dance floor courtesy of DJ Anupya.

The morning of the wedding, Parker and Karan got ready with their families and friends. “We are terrible at surprises, and he had seen my dress many times before, so I saw no purpose in a first look,” she says. The couple set off in a convertible (Parker’s hair protected in a vintage scarf from the year she was born), stopping at a vista for photos before arriving at the venue.

For her wedding look, Parker worked with Patricia Voto of One/Of to create a custom gown inspired by Christian Dior’s 1955 Soirée de Lahore. Early on, she knew she wanted something that felt like a combination of Karan and herself. “The original gown was made by the designer two years before his death and was based on a sari with the one-shoulder design and gold embroidery,” she explains. All of the embroidery was done in India, and Parker paired the gown with a custom One/Of veil featuring gold embroidery along the edge, as well as light green shoes by Paula Nadal.

Karan wore a custom Bode tuxedo with a golden sunflower detail, and as a boutonniere, he wore his own emerald kalgi (a traditional Indian headpiece for turbans). “His cufflinks and studs were my late grandfather’s, his cummerbund was unbranded vintage ’70s made in India with embellished sunflowers, and his shoes were suede Hermès.”.

Sources indicate that guests arrived to the ceremony dressed in jewel tones and metallics, walking down a pathway with giant sunflowers on either side. Parker and her mother, an amateur florist, had collaborated with Madison of Hart Floral to create the dramatic entrance. “When I spoke of our love for sunflowers and our desire to have them serve as a recurring visual throughout the day, Madison and Melissa joined forces,” Parker explains.

For the ceremony, they stood within a chuppah structure with draped gold chainmail and burgundy sunflower motifs. Karan’s best friend Drew officiated the ceremony, and the fathers of her late friends Alex and Josh read an excerpt by Ovid of the Greek myth of Baucis and Philemon. “Karan’s vows and my own were mirrors of each other. Unknowingly, we made many of the same references, and we each ended by quoting the story of Baucis and Philemon, who, when they died, received the honor of becoming intertwined as trees so they could live on forever.”.

It has been revealed that coming from mixed religious backgrounds (Karan’s parents are Sikh and Hindu and Parker’s are Episcopalian and Jewish), the couple chose to honor both. “Karan arrived on horseback as a nod to traditional Punjabi weddings. St. Christopher medallions were placed on each program, and my sister, Alison, shared a short speech about the patron saint of travelers, the namesake of the church we attended as children, and spoke about the fresh journey Karan and I were embarking upon,” Parker states. “My sister-in-law, Kareena, shared a speech about the jaimala ceremony as a nod to the Hindu wedding tradition, and spoke about the importance of seeing each other as equals.” Karan’s maternal uncle led the group in a Sikh Ardas prayer, and the ceremony ended with the Jewish tradition of the breaking of the glass. As the couple exited, guests threw dried bougainvillea from Karan’s family garden in Chandigarh.

It has been revealed that cocktail hour kicked off with oysters shipped from Island Creek Oyster Co. (the site of the couple’s first two dates). “We really wanted textiles to be an important decor motif throughout the celebration,” Parker says, noting that there was leveled seating overlaid with rugs, a rug-covered bar, and a rug-covered makeshift bandstand. Later on, their sisters shared speeches, and the couple danced to “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You,” then launching into “Dancing in the Moonlight” as tambourines were passed to guests. “Guests followed Karan and I through the field to reveal the tent, set among the cabins.”.

The band continued to play as guests entered the tent and danced. At each seat, Parker and Karan placed a letter explaining what their friendship meant to the couple. After the buzz died down, Parker’s father opened the evening with a speech. “We then had a family-style dinner of our favorite bites: kale salad, focaccia, Idaho trout, pesto gnocchi, and vodka meatballs,” she states.

In a recent development, after dinner wrapped up, Parker and her father danced to “Wide Open Spaces” (a song they listened to as she was growing up) before everyone joined in. The couple snuck away to cut the cake—a 30-inch round flourless chocolate confection covered in raspberries—which was passed out on the outskirts of the dance floor. Indian sweets called ladoos were also passed around.

Industry observers note that after a full week of wedding events between California for the traditional Indian celebration and four days in Sun Valley, the two were understandably exhausted. “It took weeks to recover, but the whole time all we could talk about was how deeply happy we were.”.

We kicked off our wedding weekend with a burgers-and-beers Western party at our favorite Sun Valley institution, Grumpy’s. We took photos in the horse pastures near town before meeting guests. —Parker.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday.
  • Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.
  • But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the newly introduced Congress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the newly introduced Congress.

According to recent reports, the conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a plan to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

It has been revealed that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., remarked the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”.

“I will vote for the delay,” he mentioned. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

“If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he stated, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”.

Sources indicate that “People are voicing opinions on all sides of the problems. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”.

No challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators said. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”.

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer said, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

In a recent development, sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., noted voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul said. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”.

Recent findings suggest that hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”.

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer mentioned.

John M. Donnelly contributed to the report.

#43078. Is Cottage Cheese Good for You?

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tasteofhome ↗ Open Full Page

Is Cottage Cheese Good for You?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yes, cottage cheese is good for you!
  • I have to admit: I can see why cottage cheese recipes go viral.
  • It has been revealed that as a dietitian and recipe developer, I love an ingredient that’s not only nutritious but also versatile and affordable, and that can help me meet my daily protein goals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Yes, cottage cheese is good for you! It's packed with protein and calcium, but the kind you buy matters. Here's how to choose the best cottage cheese for cooking, baking and snacking.

I have to admit: I can see why cottage cheese recipes go viral. TikTok trends have turned this humble dairy staple into everything from high-protein flatbread to better-for-you ice cream. Packed with protein and important vitamins and minerals, cottage cheese is an easy way to make everyday meals more satisfying.

It has been revealed that as a dietitian and recipe developer, I love an ingredient that’s not only nutritious but also versatile and affordable, and that can help me meet my daily protein goals. There are so many creative ways to use cottage cheese, and a whole fresh world of options opens up when you whip it smooth. Think: smoothies, creamy dips, pasta sauces, puddings and more!

According to recent reports, but as versatile as cottage cheese is, you can’t swap it into every recipe without a little know-how. And with so many milkfat options, the one you buy matters. I’ll share my favorite ways to use it, which varieties work best for different dishes and a few tricks to help you get delicious results every time.

First things first: Here’s why you might want to toss another tub of cottage cheese into your grocery cart.

Cottage cheese is one of my go-to high-protein foods. A half-cup serving packs 12 to 14 grams of protein, roughly the same amount you’d get from two large eggs.

Adding a scoop of cottage cheese to my plate is an easy way to make meals and snacks more satisfying without turning on the stove. I especially like it at breakfast, when it’s all too easy to end up with a meal that’s heavy on carbohydrates but light on protein. A scoop alongside toast and fruit, or blended into pancake batter, gives breakfast a little extra staying power without much effort.

You don’t have to be lifting heavy weights to care about muscle health. Our bodies need plenty of protein to maintain and repair muscle tissue, and that becomes especially important as we get older.

I like to keep cottage cheese on hand for an easy post-workout snack because there’s nothing to prep. Pair it with fruit or whole-grain crackers, and you’ve got protein plus carbohydrates to help muscles refuel and recover after exercise.

The protein in cottage cheese does more than help keep you full and support your muscles—it also plays an important role in keeping your bones strong. Cottage cheese aprovides two minerals that work together to support bone health: phosphorus and calcium.

It’s worth noting that cottage cheese contains less calcium than a serving of milk or Greek yogurt, but it can absolutely contribute to your daily intake. Just be sure to include other calcium-rich foods in your diet, too.

Emiko Franzen For Taste Of Home.

Recent findings suggest that the type of cottage cheese you buy can make a big difference in how your recipes turn out. Like other dairy products, cottage cheese comes in different milkfat percentages, which affects its taste and texture.

Sources indicate that I usually reach for 2% or 4% cottage cheese, depending on how I’m using it. Low-fat (2% cottage cheese) is perfect for whipping into dips, spreads and pasta sauces. It contains enough fat to blend smooth and creamy without feeling too heavy.

It has been revealed that full-fat, or 4% cottage cheese, gets my vote for baked goods, casseroles and lasagna fillings. The extra fat adds richness, which is especially helpful if you’re using it in place of sour cream or cream cheese.

I usually skip fat-free cottage cheese for cooking. It tends to be watery with a slightly chalky taste, and the lack of fat can make creamy recipes less satisfying. That extra moisture can also affect the texture of baked dishes, so I prefer cottage cheese with a little more fat for the best results.

In a recent development, for all its nutritional perks, cottage cheese can also pack a lot of sodium. Some brands contain more than 400 milligrams per half-cup serving. Eat a full cup, and you could be getting more than 800 milligrams of sodium (about one-third of the recommended daily limit) from cottage cheese alone.

Too much sodium can raise blood pressure and increase your risk of heart disease, so it’s worth paying attention to how much you’re getting, especially if you eat cottage cheese regularly.

If you’re watching your sodium intake, compare labels and choose a brand that’s lower in sodium. Good Culture is one of my favorite cottage cheese brands. With 380 milligrams of sodium per serving, it’s a little lower than other brands.

I also go easy on added salt when using cottage cheese with salty ingredients like Parmesan or ranch seasoning.

Julia Hartbeck for Taste of Home.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For this taste test, we sampled nine varieties of store-bought meat lasagna, cooking each from frozen and concealing the brand names from our tasters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Frozen lasagna is a meal for when you just don’t have it in you. For when you need the comfort of pasta, cheese, and sauce, but you’re not prepared to spend hours boiling, sautéing, and layering. And that’s okay. A great frozen lasagna might not hold a candle to BA’s Best Lasagna, but at the very least it should hold together, with distinct layers, plenty of sauce, gooey cheese, and bouncy pasta.

For this taste test, we sampled nine varieties of store-bought meat lasagna, cooking each from frozen and concealing the brand names from our tasters. Three stood out: Trader Joe’s tasted the closest to homemade, Marie Callender’s was a solid backup, and Rao’s was our favorite for a single serving.

After grumbling our way through several contenders and questioning mankind’s ability to produce a decent supermarket lasagna, Trader Giotto’s Family Style Meat Lasagna restored our faith with a hearty meat sauce and genuinely tasty noodles.

Why it won us over: Trader Joe’s frozen lasagna had a homemade vibe. There were distinct layers of pasta, cheese, and meaty sauce. The cheeses—ricotta, mozzarella, Romano, and Parmesan—each pulled their weight. And the noodles had a fresh bounce. “There’s a whole tomato!” exclaimed senior editor Kelsey Jane Youngman upon finding a chunk of diced tomato in her sample. Other tasters complimented the bright aromatics—fennel was prominent, backed up by oregano and basil. The evenly distributed ground beef and pork were the cherry on top.

Trader Giotto’s Family-Style Meat Lasagna, 32-oz.

More great frozen foods at Trader Joe’s →.

In a recent development, massive Lasagna would have you believe you’ll always want to cook a frozen lasagna for a crowd, but sometimes it’s about you and you alone. The 9-oz. Rao’s Made for Home Meat Lasagna is just enough for a single serving—and it doesn’t sacrifice flavor.

Why it won us over: Our tasters were excited to report that Rao’s delivered on structure. While other lasagnas were soupy, floppy, or otherwise unbalanced, Rao’s stayed intact, layer on top of layer, as we ate. It had sturdy (but not tough) noodles, a tomato sauce that was full of umami, and herbal accents that didn’t overpower. Some tasters noted a robust beefy flavor; others were more focused on the garlic and onion. Everyone went in for a second bite.

Rao’s Made-for-Home Meat Lasagna, 9-oz.

Industry observers note that maybe you don’t live by a Trader Joe’s—our condolences—and Rao’s proves elusive. You still deserve a serviceable frozen lasagna. Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce offers a sweet and tangy tomato sauce punctuated by well-seasoned meat and noodles that hold their shape.

Why it won us over: This contender avoided many of the pitfalls other brands fell into. It had a solid tomato sauce that was just slightly sweet and tangy, and the meat—both beef and sausage—was flavorful and varied enough in size to give each bite some dynamism. The pasta sheets were springy, not gummy. And while it wasn’t drowning in dairy, there was enough cottage cheese and mozzarella to make itself known.

Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce, 10.5-oz.

In a recent development, we cooked each lasagna from frozen according to its package instructions. While most contenders offered both oven and microwave directions, we stuck with the oven. Tasters sampled each lasagna without knowing which brand they were trying, evaluating each for flavor, texture, and structural integrity. Although Giovanni Rana’s Meat Lasagna is sold refrigerated, we froze it before baking, following the brand’s instructions for cooking from frozen.

The best frozen lasagna should deliver on the fundamentals of structure, flavor, and texture—a tall order for many of our contenders. That meant distinct layers; sheets of pasta that were bouncy, not flimsy; tomato sauce with concentrated flavor and enough body to cling to the pasta; meat that stood out instead of getting lost; and cheese—or many cheeses—that added milky flavor and melty cohesion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that forget the traditional opening-night fanfare. If love is a many-splendored thing, apparently it’s also bright pink and best enjoyed with a ’90s dance anthem blasting in the background.

According to recent reports, william Shakespeare’s Much Ado About Nothing arrived at the Winter Garden Theatre on Thursday with an explosion of fuchsia confetti, a giant inflatable heart, and seriously impressive dance moves from Tom Hiddleston and Hayley Atwell. Shakespeare, it seemed, was ready to party.

Following its successful run in London’s West End, the production crossed the Atlantic with Hiddleston and Atwell reprising their roles as Benedick and Beatrice, two sharp-witted characters who trade barbs before falling in love. At the show’s helm is acclaimed British director Jamie Lloyd, known for his bold, contemporary reimaginings of classic plays and musicals. With Much Ado About Nothing, he’s given Shakespeare’s romantic comedy a gloriously over-the-top makeover.

Recent findings suggest that the party started long before the curtain rose. From the moment guests stepped into the Winter Garden, ushers danced down the aisles, greeting theatergoers as though they were arriving at the hottest club. Cynthia Nixon, Rachel Zegler, Bryan Cranston, Claire Danes, Angela Bassett, Bob Odenkirk, Hugh Dancy, and Busy Philipps were among the familiar faces in the crowd, which had enough star power to rival the theatrical fireworks unfolding onstage.

Sources indicate that as Benedick and Beatrice, Hiddleston, best known to many as Marvel’s Loki, and Atwell, who played Agent Peggy Carter in the MCU, made an irresistibly mischievous pairing—dancing, singing, and flirting with infectious enthusiasm. Their characters’ courtship is one of literature’s great enemies-to-lovers stories, and the pair brought every barb, raised eyebrow, and moment of romantic tension brilliantly to life.

“I can’t do much, but I can lunge,” Hiddleston modestly told Vogue of his dancing before curtain. “The dancing is sufficiently irreverent and giddy and silly and free as this play, and I’m having the best time.”.

Dressed in a Ralph Lauren tuxedo, he described his opening-night feelings as “joyous and joyful,” declaring his love for the play, his fellow cast members, and the production. It was during his previous collaboration with Lloyd that the seeds for this one were planted. “When I was last on Broadway, for the production of Betrayal, Jamie mentioned to me on the last night, ‘What are we doing next?’ I thought he was joking and I said, ‘Much Ado About Nothing,’ and here we are!”.

Sources indicate that for Atwell, the evening marked a major milestone in her nearly 25-year acting career: she was making her Broadway debut. Clad in a chic Erdem ensemble, she reflected on the significance of the occasion shortly before taking the stage. “It’s really remarkable. It’s not lost on me how special this moment is,” she noted. “Rather than being overwhelmed by it, I really want to take it in and to cherish it.” She described herself as staying “calm amongst the excitable storm of it all.”.

Industry observers note that atwell was also having a blast with the production’s choreography, giving audiences a chance to see a different side of her. “I don’t have any formal dance training apart from going to the clubs,” she remarked, laughing. “I get to have a party every night onstage, and make moves I didn’t know I had. So it’s really fun.” The dancing came with a few occupational hazards, however, including sore knees and the occasional spill. “I’ve already slipped on my ass twice, and that felt like an initiation,” she shared. Rather than rattling her, the falls actually made her more confident: “I can survive this. I can get up and carry on.”.

Recent findings suggest that for all the fuchsia and dance-floor theatrics, the production left the Bard’s text alone. “I’ve always believed that Shakespeare should be spoken as if it was written right now or yesterday,” Hiddleston remarked. “There’s no word of this play that isn’t the 400-year-old text by Shakespeare. We have dressed it in the energy of dancing and music and levity, but the play itself is the play that it always was.”.

He went on: “Come because it will speak to your heart. This play is funny. It’s been funny for 400 years. We’ll make it easy for you.”.

Dressed in a custom pink Levi’s suit, Lloyd told Vogue that the show’s abundance of confetti—which erupts during a jubilant party scene, blanketing the stage and eventually spilling into the audience—is about more than just spectacle. “It’s certainly a lot and it’s used in a really exciting way, to show the celebration of love and joy—and that’s what the play is all about. It feels like we really need that right now.”.

The party continued well after the curtain came down. Following a standing ovation, the cast and guests headed to Tavern on the Green for the after-party, where lavish food stations served tacos, pasta, salmon, and steak skewers, while the Prosecco flowed—and, yes, people hit the dance floor.

According to recent reports, every holiday is sweeter with a tray of festive chocolate bark—and Hanukkah is no exception! This 30-minute Hanukkah bark recipe takes just a handful of ingredients and turns them into the perfect treat for sharing with friends and family as you celebrate the Festival of Lights. The surface is swirled (a lot like our marbled almond roca), and it looks as if a few dreidels were sent spinning over the melted blue candy melts and white chocolate.

It has been revealed that A tray of Hanukkah bark, decorated with an eye-catching array of colorful and shimmering sprinkles, makes a showstopping centerpiece for any Hanukkah dessert table. But it can also be a thoughtful homemade food gift you can pack into tins with a handful of chocolate gelt.

Line a 15x10x1-inch sheet pan with parchment paper.

Add the blue and white candy melts to separate microwave-safe glass bowls, then microwave at 50% power in 30-second increments, stirring after each, until smooth.

Editor’s Tip: If you’re worried about your chocolate setting too quickly, place the sheet pan in a warm oven while preparing the candy melts. A warm (but not hot) sheet pan keeps the candy melts fluid while you work, making them easier to swirl without the pressure to rush.

Industry observers note that dollop alternating spoonfuls of each color onto the parchment paper in a checkerboard pattern, leaving space between spoonfuls. Use an offset spatula to merge the colors together, then smooth them to a 1/4-inch thickness. Use a knife or wooden skewer to swirl them to create a marbled look.

Immediately sprinkle the candy melts with candy-coated chocolates and assorted sprinkles.

Recent findings suggest that transfer the pan to the refrigerator and chill the bark until it’s set. Break it into large pieces.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Store Hanukkah bark in an airtight container at room temperature for one to three weeks.

Absolutely! Hanukkah bark is a great make-ahead treat for the holiday season because it can be stored at room temperature and has a longer shelf life than many other Hanukkah desserts.

Yes, Hanukkah bark freezes well. Break it apart, then store it in an airtight, freezer-safe container for three to six months. Enjoy it straight from the freezer or defrost it at room temperature.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

According to recent reports, white chocolate and candy melts can be finicky and prone to seizing if you warm them too swiftly or at too high a temperature. If using a microwave, warm them gently on a low power setting in short increments for the best results. If you’re nervous, you can melt them on the stovetop using a double boiler or a heat-safe bowl set over a saucepan filled with 1 to 2 inches of water. If neither of those suits you, using a slow cooker or a water bath are some other ways to melt chocolate.

Yes, you can dye white chocolate. Use an oil-based or powdered type of food coloring for the best results. Gel and traditional food dyes contain too much water, which will cause the white chocolate to seize and become grainy.

Recent findings suggest that for the most eye-catching look, choose an array of sprinkles with different sizes and shapes. Varying pearl and jimmie sprinkle sizes, paired with specialty sprinkles shaped like stars, menorahs or dreidels add visual interest to the bark.

While gelt looks attractive on Hanukkah bark, foil-wrapped chocolates are difficult to remove and unwrap once they’ve been adhered to the bark. If you want to add gelt, unwrap the pieces before arranging them on the bark.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • There are few things on the Thanksgiving table that people have stronger opinions about than gravy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

It only takes a splash to give homemade gravy the rich, savory flavor you're after.

There are few things on the Thanksgiving table that people have stronger opinions about than gravy. Everyone seems to have a preferred method, a secret ingredient or a little trick they’ve been using for years. My mom has always sworn by Kitchen Bouquet, a seasoning sauce that gives gravy a little color and kick of flavor. I’m fairly certain she’s had the same bottle since the Reagan administration, and that it only comes out of the cupboard on Thanksgiving.

Sources indicate that making good turkey gravy isn’t particularly complicated, but getting that deep, rich flavor can be tricky. Even with plenty of turkey drippings and a well-made stock, sometimes it needs a little something extra. Over the years, I’ve experimented with all sorts of ways to give my gravy more flavor, but the one I come back to every time is an ingredient I always have in my pantry.

I’ve been adding a splash of soy sauce to my gravy for years, and it’s one of those little tricks that makes a noticeable difference without anyone being able to put their finger on why.

Soy sauce is rich in umami, the deeply savory flavor that makes foods like mushrooms, Parmesan cheese and the golden crust of a steak so satisfying. Adding a little soy sauce to gravy enhances those same savory flavors, giving it a richness that might otherwise require a longer cooking time. It doesn’t make your gravy taste like soy sauce, provided you use a light hand. It just makes it taste more like really good gravy.

It has been revealed that worcestershire sauce is another popular addition that works for much the same reason, bringing its own combination of savory flavor, acidity and a hint of sweetness. I’ve tried plenty of different additions over the years, and while they all have their merits, soy sauce remains my favorite. I love the depth it brings without competing with the flavors of the turkey and stock.

The trick with soy sauce is knowing when to add it and, perhaps most importantly, when to stop. You’re not trying to introduce a latest flavor to your gravy so much as coax a little more out of what’s already there. If someone can identify soy sauce in the finished product, you’ve probably been a bit too generous.

Industry observers note that I always add mine at the end, once the gravy has thickened and I’m happy with the consistency. Start with about a teaspoon for every two cups of gravy, stir it in, and give it a taste. Depending on the stock and drippings you’ve used, that may be all you need. If not, add a little more, tasting as you go.

In a recent development, one thing worth remembering is that soy sauce is salty. Very salty, in fact, so save your final seasoning adjustments until after you’ve added it. This is particularly crucial if you’re using store-bought stock, which may already contain plenty of sodium. Reduced-sodium soy sauce is an option, too, but I generally use the regular stuff and adjust accordingly.

And don’t save this trick for Thanksgiving! It works beautifully in beef and chicken gravy, too, especially when the pan drippings aren’t quite as flavorful as you’d hoped. A splash of soy sauce won’t make up for a badly made gravy, but it can do an impressive amount of work for an otherwise perfectly respectable one.

Sources indicate that have you used soy sauce in gravy before? Let us know in the comments below!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Divinity candy is a classic Southern dessert. If you haven't heard of it yet, I promise you'll be coming back to this recipe over and over again after making it just once! It’s a simple confection made of sugar, eggs, and corn syrup that looks like clouds, with the crunch of meringue and the chew of a perfect marshmallow. It does require a candy thermometer and a bit of patience, but once you know what to look for, it’s extremely simple to make.

In the large bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment, combine the egg whites and salt.

In a medium pot, combine the sugar, corn syrup, and water. Attach a candy thermometer to the pot before you go any further. Heat the mixture over medium-high heat, undisturbed, until the thermometer registers 250°, which should take about 10 minutes. When the thermometer registers 235°, start whipping egg whites on high speed until stiff peaks form, which should take another 2 to 3 minutes.

In a recent development, with the mixer running on medium speed, carefully add sugar syrup to egg whites in a thin stream. Make sure to go slowly! The whole process should take about 1 to 2 minutes. Then beat in the vanilla extract.

Proceed to increase mixer speed to high and continue to whip until the mixture comes together and loses some of its gloss, which should take approximately 5 to 10 minutes. Let it all cool until the mixture is slightly thickened and holds its form when spooned onto parchment, another 1 to 2 minutes.

Industry observers note that grease 2 spoons with cooking spray, and working promptly, spoon candy onto a parchment-lined baking sheet. Swirl it as desired to make the shapes you want! Immediately top the dessert with sprinkles. (The sprinkles won’t stick if you wait too long!).

In a recent development, let the candy sit until it’s completely dry, just about 2 hours more. Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 1 week and enjoy!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

According to recent reports, the candy can be made 1 week ahead. Store in an airtight container at room temperature.

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, noted legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

Industry observers note that “Yes, absolutely,” she stated when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”.

It has been revealed that rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, stated she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses announced a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had noted they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

In a recent development, the two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack stated she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”.

Sources indicate that “That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she stated when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this issue.”.

Sources indicate that leger Fernández said if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

Sources indicate that “We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández said. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Attendees of Bon Appétit Live experienced a taste of Maine through a hands-on lobster cooking class and a demonstration of wild blueberry cornmeal shortcakes, both hosted by Visit Maine.

Sources indicate that the class, Lobster 101, was led by Bon Appétit manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Attendees learned how to break down a whole, steamed two-pound Maine lobster and transform the meat into a rich, creamy lobster dip—ideal for holiday hosting. Guests then enjoyed the fruits of their labor, sampling the freshly made dip with Ritz crackers before tasting oysters.

Tripp explained that her oysters, cultivated in the cold tidal waters of the Lower Weskeag River, take three years to reach maturity. Known for their distinctive fluted shells, they offer a briny, mineral-rich flavor balanced by a mellow sweetness.

Sources indicate that after years as a lobster harvester, Tripp started Aphrodite Oysters to diversify her lobster business and has since shifted her focus to oyster cultivation full-time. She’s come to appreciate the many environmental benefits of farming and consuming them. Her oysters filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, taking in nitrogen and sequestering some for their growing shells. “Eating an oyster is contributing to the environment,” she declared. Indeed, water test scores have improved at her farm, demonstrating that bivalves help create a healthier ecosystem.

Before the end of the class, a few brave attendees volunteered to shuck their first oysters. Krista guided them through the process, demonstrating how to safely do it at home by protecting the hand holding the shellfish with a towel and gently working the knife into the hinge until the shell released. The well-earned reward was another taste of the Penobscot Bay, as fresh and pristine as the waters themselves.

Later in the day, guests in the Demo Kitchen were treated to Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote, prepared by Bon Appétit senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk. The compote featured wild Maine blueberries from Brodis Blueberries, a multigenerational family farm in Hope, Maine, stewarded by Ron Howard and his family. Howard joined Szewczyk for the demo, where he shared that 99% of the wild blueberries grown and harvested in the United States come from Maine. Attendees learned that they have been growing since the end of the Ice Age, when the tenacious plants, fortified by ericoid mycorrhizal fungi, began to grow and colonize the newly exposed land as glaciers retreated. An important food source for Native Americans, wild blueberries were valued by Indigenous communities for their nutritional benefits well before the modern superfood movement.

Speaking passionately, Howard discussed the many challenges facing Maine growers, including tariffs and currency exchange fluctuations, particularly the impact of a stronger Canadian dollar. Like many Maine farmers, the family has had to get creative. Howard invested in latest equipment, including a more efficient type of harvester that allowed the business to scale up and sell to retailers. They created a shelf-stable, freeze-dried product with no added ingredients, allowing them to ship their product beyond the local area. Howard and his son started a distillery, where they use wild blueberries to make an eau de vie and vodka. They have also begun hosting a Wild Blueberry Weekend, opening the doors to the farm and educating the public about the unique benefits of their crop and their growing process.

Carolann Ouellette, director of the Maine Office of Tourism, emphasized that visiting Maine and engaging with local growers and producers such as Howard and Tripp was the best way to experience the state’s diverse bounty. “The relationship between people and nature is inseparable, and stewardship is an vital part of the state's identity,” she reflected. Ouellette grew up in Upcoming Jersey but relocated to Maine over 40 years ago. Her family used to visit Maine when she was a child, and she recalls those experiences vividly: “As a kid, I remember, when you get to Maine, you can smell the pie or smell the spruce.” It’s those potent memories that drew her to the state permanently, a place she described as “filled with hardworking, welcoming communities that depend on one another.”.

According to recent reports, A few years ago, Visit Maine began placing greater emphasis on the state’s culinary identity. Ouellette said that awareness of Maine as a food destination continues to grow, “Sea to table with local ingredients is what we were doing before it was a thing.” Beyond the lobster, Visit Maine has been intentional about showcasing the breadth of the state’s agricultural, fishing, and heritage industries. Apples, potatoes, kelp, seaweed, and grains are just a few of the local ingredients featured in Visit Maine’s newsletter and Bountiful Plate video series, which highlights food and beverage producers throughout the state. Ouellette noted that Maine’s food culture is more diverse than many people expect, and its abundance of local products has attracted an interesting mix of exceptional chefs, many of whom are deeply embedded in their communities. Ouellette cited Tripp’s practice of personally delivering her oysters to local restaurants as an example of how the hospitality ecosystem is interconnected.

Most notable, Ouellette emphasized that sustainability and stewardship are central to the state’s approach to its food systems and relationship with the landscape. “You can’t get much fresher than food in Maine,” she concluded.

Latest Update: The Unstoppable Cecilia Vicuña

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a perfect fall day, bright and brisk, when I meet the Chilean artist and poet Cecilia Vicuña at her studio in Tribeca, just a few blocks away from the loft she’s lived in for the last 46 years.
  • It has been revealed that as someone so closely tethered to the natural world, Vicuña wishes we could go outside and enjoy it.
  • Vicuña, 78, is a seeker of many things: truth, justice, beauty, connection with people and the earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a perfect fall day, bright and brisk, when I meet the Chilean artist and poet Cecilia Vicuña at her studio in Tribeca, just a few blocks away from the loft she’s lived in for the last 46 years.

It has been revealed that as someone so closely tethered to the natural world, Vicuña wishes we could go outside and enjoy it. We can, I offer—there’s no reason to stay cooped up inside for our entire conversation. Grinning, she agrees to show me her studio first. “And then we seek the sun.”.

Vicuña, 78, is a seeker of many things: truth, justice, beauty, connection with people and the earth. For more than five decades she has brought attention to under-recognized voices through her sculptures, paintings, poems, videos, sound installations, and performances. For many of those years she worked in relative obscurity, known in certain avant-garde and activist circles in New York and South America, but unacknowledged by the establishment. But the global art world woke up to her brilliance about a decade ago, especially when her quipus—hanging sculptures made from wool that nod to the ancient Andean knot systems—attracted attention at Documenta 14 in Germany and Greece.

In a recent development, “Everything else disappeared next to it,” says gallerist Rachel Lehmann of the one she saw in Athens. Needing to know more about the artist of this magnificent work, she paid Vicuña a visit back in Upcoming York, and Lehmann Maupin began representing her in 2018. Since then it’s been a swift rise. In 2022, Vicuña was awarded the Venice Biennale’s Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement, one of the most prestigious prizes in contemporary art.

Vicuña’s studio, a “little hideout,” she calls it, is filled with sacred begonias, money trees, and aloe plants. During my visit she’s preparing for two new exhibitions, one on each coast of the US. On November 15, the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles unveiled “The Dream of Water: Quipu of Encounters Maricunga,” a multipart commission tied to the inaugural Eric and Wendy Schmidt Environment and Art Prize. And on November 19, Lehmann Maupin opened a show in New York City of several new Vicuña paintings and a video alongside the work of Surrealist painter Leonora Carrington, the first time their artwork will be in direct dialogue. (All this on the heels of Vicuña’s first major exhibition in the UK, at the moment on view at Whitechapel Gallery in London after appearing in Dublin, and a show in MASS MoCA that opened in the spring.).

The quipus are Vicuña’s best-known works. While a quipu can take physical form, often in vibrant strands of wool with knots intuitively tied at various intervals that hang from the ceiling and pool at the floor, its spirit extends far beyond sculpture. “From the Western perspective, quipu is an object that you find on an archeological mission. But from my perspective, it’s a way of being,” she notes. “It’s a way of connecting yourself to other people, to the land, to the future. The quipu begins when I start thinking about it.”.

There’s one thing in particular she’s been thinking about for the MoCA exhibition, which underpins its many components: the ecological crisis unfolding in the Maricunga salt flats in Chile’s Atacama Desert, brought on by lithium mining. Lithium is often referred to as white gold for its use in the batteries that power the green energy revolution. But the extraction methods are a direct threat to the already scarce water supply of the Indigenous Colla people, as well as the ancient microorganisms and parinas, or flamingos, that call the region home.

Protection of Indigenous culture has long been at the core of Vicuña’s practice. As a young girl, decades before it was confirmed by a DNA test, Vicuña knew she had American Indian blood, and indeed her mother’s side traces back to the Diaguita people. The fight against colonialism, patriarchy, environmental collapse—it’s all personal to her.

“Cecilia was very clear about what she wanted to do” with the project, says José Luis Blondet, a senior curator at MoCA who organized the show with curatorial assistant Ariana Rizo and environmental adviser Kelsey Shell. Vicuña made two trips to the Atacama Desert to connect with artists, scientists, Indigenous leaders, musicians, and others to perform rituals together, a collective intention-setting. “I believe we have to dream a different culture,” she says. “Dream from the Indigenous perspective is the way to create realities. So you dream with the intent that the dream will be a seed.”.

Scenes from her visits will replay at MoCA in a poetic five-channel video installation. Nearby, in the museum’s tallest gallery, hangs Parina Quipu, a 30-foot-long work of skeins of unspun wool in vibrant pinks with bits of brown and gray streaked in, mimicking the dramatic Martian landscape of the Atacama. “The beauty there is divine,” Vicuña says.

Sources indicate that the third component of the MoCA show will arrive next spring with a series of performances and rituals, a Vicuña specialty that she calls a “quipu of encounters.” For this one, she’ll gather Los Angeles water guardians and her collaborators like Cristina Dorador, an acclaimed Chilean scientist whose ongoing study of the Atacama Desert’s microbial life was crucial to Vicuña’s understanding of the crisis there. “What is happening at the Atacama Desert is happening right here, right now,” states Blondet. “Different version, different elements, but it’s the same struggle.”.

In addition to her quipus, the key to understanding Vicuña’s work is arte precario, the term she invented for the poignant little configurations she started making back in the 1960s out of bits of trash. She was still living in Chile then, not yet 20 years old.

Sources indicate that “Precario means what is fragile, what might disappear,” she tells me as we sit in her studio, her voice soft (she gets much louder when she laughs, which is often). “But it disappears to regenerate life, to regenerate potentials. To stay in the potential—that’s what precario means.”.

Sources indicate that she has experienced plenty of precariousness herself. In 1972 she traveled to London to attend the Slade School of Fine Art on a scholarship. The following year a military coup overthrew the democratically elected Chilean president, Salvador Allende, and a brutal dictatorship under Augusto Pinochet began. People she knew back home were tortured, disappeared. Her father lost his job managing public pensions. It wasn’t safe to return, so she sought asylum in England, and in London she cofounded an organization called Artists for Democracy in solidarity with liberation struggles in Chile and around the world.

Industry observers note that precarios may represent instability, but they are also doused in hope. “When you’re aware of your death and your fragility, it’s like you acquire a different kind of power,” Vicuña says. “There’s a new freedom because you cease to be afraid. And you can be absolutely joyful, because there’s air to breathe.”.

The Lehmann Maupin show this fall highlights an important kinship between Vicuña and Leonora Carrington. Vicuña stayed with Carrington in Mexico City in 1969 on her way back to Chile from New York. Though 31 years apart in age, the two connected easily. “We had this really beautiful encounter,” she remembers. Carrington had read the young Vicuña’s poems, which had been published in a Mexican poetry magazine when she was a teenager, while Carrington was already a star in Mexico City’s avant-garde scene.

Vicuña was only there a few days, but her friend Coca Roccatagliata, also a Chilean artist, stayed with Carrington even longer and learned her techniques of translating visions into paintings—called calcomanías—which she passed along to Vicuña once back in Chile.

Industry observers note that “I think this was major,” states Lehmann. More framework than set of rules, Carrington’s tips helped Vicuña transfer the pictures in her head onto canvas. She went on to make figurative paintings in a style that mashed up Surrealism with folklore, politics, and eroticism.

Many of Vicuña’s early paintings were lost in the years of Chile’s dictatorship. Recently she has set about remaking them, often from memory. Her Medusa at Lehmann Maupin has two dates: 1972, for the original, and 2023, when it was re-created.

The brand-newly introduced paintings are no less affecting, and pair well with mysterious Carrington works like Eye Witness from 1987, made when she was 70. Vicuña’s Dos Trenzas demonstrates a woman with two long braids skipping toward a mountain. Cuatro Lideresas depicts four Indigenous women leaders. Vicuña had in mind the two months she spent hitchhiking through the Amazon in 1977, when the Trans-Amazonian Highway was not yet complete. “There would be highway, and then a river four times as immense. And they had no bridge, nothing. So you had to wait there until a sort of little balsa”—a raft—“would come from the other side, maybe today, maybe tomorrow.”.

As promised, we make our way out of the studio and into the autumn air. Winding through Tribeca to get to the Hudson River, which she does every day, she remarks on how much the neighborhood has changed since she moved here in 1980. It was dark, no lights, few people, rubble everywhere. She’d wriggle through a fence to get to the water’s edge back then, collecting basuritas, little trash, to make her precarios.

I ask if picking things up from the ground has ever gotten her in trouble. There was one time, around the mid-’80s, when she was weaving weeds and debris atop pools of water on the pavement. “I heard this breath behind me,” she states. It was a police horse. “What are you doing here, young lady? This is illegal,” she remembers the officer saying. And then who shows up but the artist Richard Tuttle, a neighbor. “He starts scolding the policeman and tells him, ‘She is a very well-known artist.’ It was completely untrue! Nobody knew me at that time.”.

We arrive at one of her favorite spots at Hudson River Park, where the pier narrows to a point. Nimble as a teenager, she drops to her stomach to look out at the water from as close a vantage point as possible, and beckons me to join. “Isn’t this like being in a boat?” she asks.

She tells me about the confluence of the Hudson’s two currents. “The Native name for the river is River That Flows Both Ways,” she notes. “And you can certainly see when they’re in the middle, fighting—finally, one wins.”.

“The Dream of Water: Quipu of Encounters Maricunga” is on view at MoCA Grand Avenue in Los Angeles through June 6, 2027. “Leonora Carrington & Cecilia Vicuña” is on view at Lehmann Maupin gallery in Upcoming York City through December 19, 2026.

Fall baking has a way of leaving you with awkward amounts of leftover canned pumpkin. So many recipes call for half a can or some other quantity that leaves you wondering what exactly you’re supposed to do with the rest. You put the open can of Libby’s pumpkin puree in the refrigerator with every intention of using it, yet a few days later, there it is, still waiting for you to come up with a plan. It’s not as though you can make half a pumpkin pie.

In a recent development, fortunately, you don’t need much pumpkin to make something wonderful. In fact, one of the best things I’ve made with leftover pumpkin requires less than a cup, a handful of pantry staples and very little effort. It’s the sort of recipe that makes having leftover pumpkin feel less like a nuisance and more like a stroke of good luck.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

It has been revealed that these are a little different from the dense, chewy blondies you might be accustomed to. They have golden edges and a wonderfully soft, almost cakey center, thanks in part to the pumpkin puree. Brown sugar gives them their rich, buttery sweetness, while cinnamon and pumpkin pie spice make them taste unmistakably like fall. The recipe lists the chocolate chips as optional, though I’d argue strongly in favor of including them. Chocolate and pumpkin are excellent together, and the little pockets of melted chocolate are delicious against all those warm spices.

Industry observers note that the pumpkin blondies also almost suspiciously easy to make. Everything comes together in one bowl, using ingredients you probably already have on hand. There’s no frosting to fuss with, no dough to chill and no pie crust to negotiate. Just spread the batter into a 9-inch pan and bake it for 25 to 30 minutes. You’ll have a dozen soft, spiced bars that are equally at home on a Thanksgiving dessert table as they are next to your morning coffee.

Recent findings suggest that best of all, the recipe calls for just 1/2 cup of canned pumpkin. That’s a particularly convenient amount when you’ve got the remains of another baking project taking up residence in the refrigerator. And if you have a full cup left, making a double batch seems like a perfectly reasonable course of action.

Industry observers note that and there’s no reason to limit pumpkin to sweet recipes. A few spoonfuls can add body and richness to soups, pasta dishes and risotto, especially when paired with sage, garlic and Parmesan. Just be sure you’re using plain pumpkin puree rather than pumpkin pie filling, which already contains sugar and spices and isn’t as versatile.

Sources indicate that if you’re not quite ready to commit to another pumpkin project, you can always freeze your leftover pumpkin puree. That way, the next time a recipe calls for an odd amount of pumpkin, you’ll have some on hand.

There are a lot of ways to adapt this chicken Alfredo recipe using up other ingredients you might have on hand. Make it with chicken breasts as written, or swap in chicken thighs or leftover rotisserie chicken instead. Use fresh broccoli or pull those frozen florets from the freezer. Spice up the Parmesan sauce with a little extra cayenne pepper, or add a swirl of herby pesto.

It has been revealed that cook the fettuccine according to the package directions for al dente. Add the broccoli florets to the water for the last five minutes of cooking.

Meanwhile, in a large skillet, cook the chicken and chopped onion in butter until the chicken is no longer pink. Add the minced garlic, salt and cayenne pepper, and cook for one minute longer. Stir in the flour until it’s blended with the other ingredients.

Recent findings suggest that gradually add the half-and-half, thawed peas and Parmesan cheese to the skillet. Bring the mixture to a boil. Cook and stir the sauce for one to two minutes or until it’s thickened.

According to recent reports, drain the fettuccine and broccoli, and toss them with the chicken mixture. Serve the chicken broccoli Alfredo while it’s hot.

Once the chicken broccoli Alfredo cools, transfer it to a sealed food storage container. Store it in the refrigerator for up to four days.

Yes, you can prepare this dish up to three days ahead of time. Gently reheat the chicken broccoli Alfredo in a covered skillet on the stove.

Recent findings suggest that the creamy sauce in this Alfredo recipe may separate and turn watery when frozen and then thawed. To protect the texture, it’s best not to freeze chicken broccoli Alfredo.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that inspired by the iconic egg and sausage sandwich on a pancake bun, this breakfast casserole is cheesy and just a smidge sweet from the brushing of maple butter at the very end. Destined for holiday brunch tables everywhere and best enjoyed while you’re still in pajamas, this cozy bake will feed a full house. (Don’t be surprised if you find yourself making it again long after the last guest leaves though!).

More high-protein breakfast recipes here.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Lightly coat a 13x9" baking dish with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Whisk 2½ cups (313 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 Tbsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Set aside.

According to recent reports, cook 2 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, in a large skillet set over medium-high heat, stirring and breaking into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind. Pour fat into a heatproof measuring glass. You want ½ cup fat; spoon out any excess or pour in vegetable oil as needed if you don’t have enough. Stir 2 large eggs and 2 cups whole milk into fat. Let sausage cool slightly, then crumble into small, even pieces with your hands.

Pour fat mixture into reserved dry ingredients and stir until just combined and no large dry pockets of flour remain (batter may be thin and lumpy; it’ll be fine). Set aside ½ cup sausage and ½ cup cheese from 8 oz. sharp yellow cheddar, coarsely grated (about 2 cups), for topping, then add remaining sausage and cheddar to batter and stirring until evenly distributed.

Scrape batter into prepared baking dish and evenly scatter reserved sausage and cheese over. Bake casserole until top springs back when gently pressed with your finger and a tester inserted into the center comes out with just a few moist crumbs attached, 20–30 minutes.

Just before casserole is done, heat 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a small skillet over medium, stirring occasionally, until butter is melted, about 2 minutes.

Brush maple butter over casserole and let cool 10 minutes. Cut into squares. Serve with more maple syrup and butter alongside.

Industry observers note that in the caption, Fieri described Jim as his hero and expressed how much he still misses him. Fans swiftly filled the comments with condolences and support.

Sources indicate that “Sending love on this special day,” one user wrote. On Facebook, another commented, “I hope your memories of your dad comfort you today. He must have been so proud of you.”.

Industry observers note that others shared their own happy memories of Jim. “I miss the stories and conversations with this man,” one person wrote. “He was the best!!” Another recalled, “Jim was a true romantic. I'll never forget when he made the rose petal trail for your mom.”.

Fieri has been open about how deeply the loss affected him. “I wanna call him all the time and ask questions, help me solve problems or celebrate the wins,” he said in a series of Instagram Stories last year. “Wouldn’t be here if it weren’t for him and it's hard to be here without him.”.

Industry observers note that birthdays, anniversaries, and holidays are still hard for Fieri, but he’s also found some comfort in his family. Industry News: Nigella Lawson’s Best Baking Advice Of All Time

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there are few people I trust more in the kitchen than Nigella Lawson.
  • From the kitchen hacks you’d never expect (like swapping milk for boiling water) to the little techniques that make all the difference in your final bake, this is Nigella Lawson’s best baking advice of all time.
  • It has been revealed that cooking might not require exact measurements, but baking definitely does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there are few people I trust more in the kitchen than Nigella Lawson. If she told me to put sardines in a birthday cake, I’d believe her. That’s just the kind of culinary authority you earn after nearly three decades of making us hungry through the TV screen. The cookbook author and television personality is now dishing out advice on The Great British Baking Show—she made her debut as a GBBS judge in September—but it’s just a small window into her extensive wisdom.

From the kitchen hacks you’d never expect (like swapping milk for boiling water) to the little techniques that make all the difference in your final bake, this is Nigella Lawson’s best baking advice of all time.

It has been revealed that cooking might not require exact measurements, but baking definitely does. “I think every recipe has to be as precise as possible,” Lawson told Vogue in 2018. “Baking, you have to be really precise. If you’re cooking and it suggests 2 to 3 carrots, it doesn’t really matter because they can be different sizes. It’s not going to alter the taste.”.

Sources indicate that so, you’ve never really baked before. It’s okay to start small! A three-tier chantilly cake your first day in the kitchen probably isn’t your best bet. “It’s important to go for a simple recipe. Read through the recipe to make sure you understand everything that’s being told to you at the time,” she stated. “Look for a recipe that gives you an indication of what to do at each stage. This is what I always say to people: remind yourself you’re not running a restaurant.”.

Industry observers note that if you’ve been making your chocolate cake with milk, here’s your sign to stop. Lawson suggests swapping the dairy for hot or boiling water instead to “bloom” the cocoa, dissolve the sugar, and loosen the batter. The result? A crazy moist crumb!

Sources indicate that instead of using plain water when baking bread, Lawson suggests swapping it out for leftover pasta or potato water. “It will help the bread’s texture and rise,” she wrote on X in 2020. “Taste it before adding, though. If very salty, dilute it with fresh water and, obviously, leave any salt in the recipe out.”.

Sources indicate that it might sound weird, but Lawson swears by cream of tartar for fluffier, softer scones. “These are the best [ones] I’ve ever eaten, which is quite how it should be since they emanate from one of those old-fashioned cooks who starts a batch the minute the doorbell rings at teatime,” she wrote on her website in 2017. “Yes, I know they look as if they’ve got cellulite—it’s the cream of tartar, which is also why, despite their apparent solidity, they have that dreamy lightness.”.

Recent findings suggest that lawson’s genius baking hack? DIY self-rising flour. “Nigella tends not to use self-raising flour in her more recent books as she doesn’t bother to keep both plain (all-purpose) and self-raising flour,” her site reads. “Partly because keeping just one type of flour saves on storage space, and partly because if you don’t use self-raising flour regularly, then it will lose its raising power over time.”.

According to recent reports, instead, simply add 2 teaspoons of baking powder for each cup of plain flour. Sift the flour and baking powder together into a bowl before using (and make sure the baking powder is fully integrated), and you’re golden!

We’re all a little extra busy around the holidays, so if you’re planning a dinner party or holiday get-together, it’s okay to make shortcuts. Even Lawson indicates not everything has to be baked from scratch.

“I have a bit of a weakness for this sort of cake, which is essentially an assembly-job number, a construction of alternate layers of a rich, boozy cream and some store-bought sponge or other,” she told the BBC in 2023 about one of her favorite holiday desserts. “Here the layers comprise a confection of cream and mascarpone, seasonally spiked with Advocaat, full of crystallized ginger, figs and nuts, and that essential component of Christmas: gingerbread.”.

Even Lawson admits: “just the words ‘uniformity of size and shape’ make [her] quake.” Hello, crazy foreshadowing for her future on GBBS.

“I am not in the slightest bit insecure about what I can bake, and I’m so very happy doing it, but shop-bought perfection is way beyond me,” she said in a 2014 interview with The Guardian. “But I’m perfectly content with that, and with the ramshackle homemade-ness of my creations.” If that’s good enough for Nigella, it’s good enough for me!
