This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that binary stars are common in the Milky Way.
  • Astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs).
  • It has been revealed that it all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that binary stars are common in the Milky Way. Up to 40% Milky Way stars are binaries, though there's a lack of absolute certainty. Sirius, which is the brightest star in the night sky, is actually a binary star.

Astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs). It means that a body of gas surrounds both stars, but the gas doesn't move with either one separately. These envelopes are transitory; the CE creates drag that slowly draws the planets together, sometimes ending in an explosion. But it's difficult to predict when that will happen, and when astronomers should observe a particular binary star to learn more about it.

It has been revealed that it all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars. No two stars in a binary system are the same. One evolves and puffs up, overflowing its Roche lobe. Mass begins to pile up on its companion. That process becomes unstable, and the two stars become engulfed in a common envelope of gas.

The common envelope exerts a powerful drag on both stars, and they're drawn closer together. After that, the CE is ejected and the two stars are left behind in a compact binary. The pair of tightly-bound stars can remain as a compact binary, or they can merge and cause an explosion, called a luminous red nova(LRN). Whether they merge and explode, or whether they remain as a compact binary, depends on how soon the CE is ejected. If the CE isn't dissipated soon enough, the continued drag forces the stars closer together until they merge and erupt.

This simple graphic shows how common envelopes evolve. At first, on star fills its Roche lobe. Then, the companion is engulfed and both stars orbit one another inside the common envelope. Then, either the common envelope is ejected and the stars remain as a binary, or the common envelope isn't ejected, and the stars are forced to merge. Image Credit: By Philip D. Hall - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/55287112.

In a recent development, this is a coarse overview of the process. Astronomers know it can happen, and they'd like to learn more about it. But they need to observe them, and that's tough to do. Not only are they difficult to predict, but they're also relatively rare.

Industry observers note that observations with the JWST and other telescopes have found one CE situation where a main sequence star a little less massive than the Sun spiralled into its CE partner, a puffy supergiant star, and erupted as a LRN. This happened in our neighbouring galaxy, Andromeda. The observations and details are in fresh research in Nature titled "An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion." The first author is Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York.

"The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars," the authors write. "This is theorized to happen via Common Envelope Evolution, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag.".

That much is known by astrophysical theory. But nobody's observed the end of the inspiral and the eruption yet. "Here, we present observations of ATâ2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy," the researchers write.

Astronomers have lots of observations of ATâ2025abao with multiple telescopes because it's been experiencing brightness changes for several years and has attracted their attention. They've become familiar with ATâ2025abao and now simply refer to it as 'Bao'.

Recent findings suggest that âStellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,â remarked first author Karambelkar. âHowever, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the starsâ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescopeâs data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.â.

It has been revealed that stars in these situations orbit each other for thousands of years with little change, and that was true of ATâ2025abao. But once they contacted each other, things changed. Other stars in CEs take thousands of orbits before they merge. But this one was different from other CE binaries. The pair merged after only 7 orbits (about 7 years.).

Observations go back as far as 2018, and between then and early 2025, the star gradually brightened in optical light. After that, it gradually faded in optical light, but its infrared light continued to brighten. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. It brightened by 100 times in the r-band over a period 25 days, and its temperature jumped to about 8000 Kelvin. Then, for about 80 days it plateaued and cooled down to about 3000 Kelvin. The JWST observed it during this period, only 47 days after its peak.

âWe thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,â said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. âOne day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!â.

Recent findings suggest that âWhen a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect â a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Baoâs data,â remarked co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in Fresh York. âAs the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary starâs outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.â.

According to recent reports, this was when the CEE began. The primary star engulfed the companion star in a common envelope, and drag stole its momentum, forcing it to spiral inward. This is when the JWST saw the destructive merger.

This is the finding chart for AT 2025abao. It was captured by the Asiago 67/92cm Schmidt telescope on 7 November 2025, when the light was at is maximum. M 31's (Andromeda) spiral disk is just visible on the left of the image. The zoomed-in panel shows the transient. Image Credit: Reguitti et al. A&A, 709, A25 (2026).

Since the transient has been in the watchful eyes of astronomers for so long, they have detailed spectroscopy from it. The SPHEREx near-infrared space observatory played an notable role, catching the star in its survey. "In July 2025, the source was serendipitously observed during its rapid optical fading by the first sky survey of the SPHEREx mission, providing a precise glimpse of the stellar photosphere during this phase," the researchers state. That let them determine the masses of the stars, but only with some help from simulations.

Sources indicate that as in a lot of astronomy research, simulations played an important role here. In this research, the authors worked with different models of CEE until the outcome of one matched the JWST's detailed observations of the star and its surrounding dust, shed by the primary star over hundreds of years.

That work revealed that the primary was seven times more massive than the Sun, with a radius 350 times larger. It was also 18,000 times brighter than our star. âIt was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,â said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

Recent findings suggest that the modelling also revealed the smaller star's true nature. It had only about 0.7 solar masses, one-tenth as massive as the other star. Its radius was much smaller and it was also much dimmer.

The astronomers called the pair Big Bao and Little Bao, and when Little Bao was engulfed, there was a massive explosion. Only more observations will reveal what the resulting star, now simply called Bao, looks like.

These artist's illustrations help explain what happened with ATâ2025abao and its common envelope evolution. The first panel demonstrates the quiescent phase, when the stars are surrounded by a common envelope. The brightness was consistent during this phase. The second panel shows the stars brightening in the precursor stage. The companion star experiences drag and begins to spiral toward the primary star. In the third panel, there's a sudden bright eruption, as the companion spiralled and the common envelope is ejected. The JWST observed this. Then, in the final panel, months after the eruption, gas from the starâs ejected envelope freely expanded at the poles, but not at the equator, where previous ejecta from the more massive star was concentrated. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia).

Sources indicate that "The 2025 eruption of ATâ2025abao displays the defining hallmarks of Luminous Red Novae, a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection into a common envelope during the merger of a star with its companion," the authors write. But it's different from all other known LRN. It's progenitor is unambiguously an evolved AGB star with an extended convective envelope.

Industry observers note that "In contrast, all known LRN progenitors have primary stars on the main sequence," the researchers explain. But classical CEE theory claims that the primary star should be an AGB star.

"Thus, ATâ2025abao provides the first view of a classical CEE progenitor system continuously monitored from its onset through its culmination," the authors explain.

Watching a common envelope evolution in real time like this is a first in astronomy. Astronomers have had to perform a sort of forensic astrophysical study of transients like this in other cases, trying to reconstruct what happened thousands or even millions of years ago. Even with powerful telescopes and computer simulations, and with detailed theoretical frameworks to guide their work, that's tough to do.

Sources indicate that but this work opens a new window into CEE and how efficient it can be. And it's just in time to help with a potential flood of upcoming transient detections. Only a few dozen luminous red novae have been detected, but the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time will detect hundreds of them, possibly thousands. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will also detect some LRN and CEE, but probably far fewer.

This work lays the foundation for understanding some of what those surveys will find. In a few years time, astronomers should have a much clearer understanding of common envelope evolution and luminous red novae.

"This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys," the authors write.

#42952. Why Sleeping 9 Hours After 50 May Be a Warning Sign for Your Career

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1208 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Why Sleeping 9 Hours After 50 May Be a Warning Sign for Your Career

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More sleep does not necessarily mean more years at work, as a large Finnish study links both restless nights and unusually long sleep to shorter working lives.
  • As retirement ages rise and people are expected to work later into life, researchers are looking more closely at what helps people remain in the workforce as they grow older.
  • Sources indicate that people with severe sleep disturbances could expect to spend around eight fewer months in the workforce than those who rarely experienced sleep problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More sleep does not necessarily mean more years at work, as a large Finnish study links both restless nights and unusually long sleep to shorter working lives.

As retirement ages rise and people are expected to work later into life, researchers are looking more closely at what helps people remain in the workforce as they grow older. A large Finnish study suggests that sleep may be part of the picture. Adults who frequently struggled with sleep after age 50 tended to spend fewer years working, while those who regularly slept nine hours or more a night also had shorter expected working lives.

Sources indicate that people with severe sleep disturbances could expect to spend around eight fewer months in the workforce than those who rarely experienced sleep problems. Among people who slept at least nine hours a night, the gap ranged from roughly nine months to more than two years, depending on the study group.

Sources indicate that the findings, published online in Occupational & Environmental Medicine, come as more than half of the countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) have raised statutory retirement ages in response to aging populations. Previous research has explored why people leave their jobs early, including disability, illness, and retirement decisions. However, researchers had not examined whether sleep duration and quality were associated with how long people remain employed.

To investigate, the team focused on working life expectancy, which measures the average number of years someone can expect to remain employed at a particular age. Rather than measuring how long people live, the researchers examined their expected years in the workforce between ages 50 and 68.

The analysis drew on two Finnish studies involving more than 76,000 adults. The Finnish Public Sector (FPS) study included 70,339 public sector employees between 2000 and 2016, approximately 80% of whom were women. The Health and Social Support (HeSSup) study provided a random sample of 6,071 working-age Finnish adults between 1998 and 2013, with women accounting for 54% of participants. Researchers assessed sleep using the first survey each participant completed after turning 50, then examined employment information from the Earnings and Accrual Register, maintained by the Finnish Centre for Pensions.

Sources indicate that the surveys asked participants how long they usually slept and how often they experienced difficulties falling asleep, staying asleep, waking too early, or feeling unrested after sleeping. These disturbances were assessed over the preceding four weeks. People who experienced them no more than once a week were considered to have no sleep disturbances, while those reporting problems two to four nights a week were placed in the moderate category. Severe disturbances meant experiencing these problems five or six nights a week to nearly every night. Sleep duration was classified separately as short, meaning less than seven hours, mid-range at seven to eight and a half hours, or long at nine hours or more.

Sources indicate that the results revealed a consistent relationship between disrupted sleep and fewer expected years of employment. Participants without sleep disturbances had an average working life expectancy of 13 years and five months after age 50. That fell to approximately 13 years among those with moderate disturbances and 12 years and 10 months among those with severe problems. Compared with people reporting no disturbances, these groups could expect to work nearly five and eight fewer months, respectively. The association appeared among both men and women and across three broad occupational categories: professional, intermediate, and routine jobs.

It has been revealed that employment differences became more apparent when researchers examined sleep alongside occupation and sex. Professional women who reported no sleep disturbances had the longest expected working lives in this comparison, at nearly 14 years after age 50. Men in routine jobs who experienced severe sleep disturbances had the shortest, at approximately 12 and a half years.

Sources indicate that sleep duration revealed a somewhat different pattern. In the Finnish Public Sector study, participants sleeping fewer than seven hours a night and those sleeping between seven and eight and a half hours had the same average working life expectancy of 13 years and two months. Those who regularly slept nine hours or more, however, had an expected working life of just 12 years and five months. Compared with the mid-range sleep group, that represented approximately nine fewer months of employment.

According to recent reports, the association was even stronger in the HeSSup study, where sleeping nine hours or more was linked to just over 30 fewer months of expected employment compared with sleeping seven to eight and a half hours. Researchers found no clear evidence that people sleeping fewer than seven hours had shorter working lives than those in the mid-range category, regardless of sex or job type.

Education and occupation also appeared to shape these patterns. When researchers compared the most advantaged participants, those with professional jobs or higher education and no sleep disturbances or short to mid-range sleep, with the least advantaged, those in routine jobs or with lower education and severe sleep problems or long sleep, the differences were considerable. The gap in expected working life was approximately one year and five months in the FPS group and five years in the HeSSup group.

In a recent development, in a more detailed analysis combining sleep duration with socioeconomic circumstances, 50-year-old men and women in professional jobs who reported short nightly sleep had the longest expected working lives in the FPS study, at around 13 years and seven months. In HeSSup, highly educated women had the longest working life expectancy, at approximately 11 and a half years. At the other extreme, men in routine jobs or with lower levels of education who regularly slept nine hours or more had an expected working life of only about six years and five months in both study groups.

Although the findings suggest a connection between sleep and working life, they do not establish that poor sleep or longer sleep directly causes people to leave employment earlier. The study was observational, and the researchers could not account for several potentially influential factors, including physical and mental health, underlying medical conditions, risky health behaviors, and working conditions such as shift work. These factors could affect both sleep patterns and the ability to remain employed.

Still, the findings suggest that helping people manage sleep problems in midlife may be worth considering as countries look for ways to support longer working careers, particularly among people facing socioeconomic disadvantages.

“Promoting sleep health and providing support for managing sleep disturbances at midlife may be especially important for those with a lower socioeconomic status when aiming to increase workforce participation with advancing age,” the researchers concluded.

“This could include cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia delivered by occupational health services or workplace interventions, such as educational or health promotion interventions for sleep.”.

Sources indicate that reference: “Sleep disturbances and sleep duration as predictors of working life expectancy among adults aged 50 years and older in Finland” by Saana Myllyntausta, Katriina Heikkilä, Jaana Pentti, Holendro Singh Chungkham, Sakari Suominen, Mika Kivimaki, Jussi Vahtera, Paola Zaninotto, Jenni Ervasti and Sari Stenholm, 18 August 2026, Occupational and Environmental Medicine. DOI: 10.1136/oemed-2025-110766.
